cells.tense: A second stream is arriving right now, and the joining is being chosen with a steady hand rather than drifted into.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's entering this month and say plainly, once, that you've chosen it — then throw one hour at it and let that be enough.
cells.core:
You can tell what's genuinely arriving from what's only drifting past. You meet it with your eyes on its shape, not on where it could carry you, and the joining happens because it's chosen, not because it's convenient. That reading of what's in front of you holds, and it shapes how you meet the next thing.

What's entering now is a second stream, and you're deciding it rather than sliding into it. That's how it looks at this doorway: no small act this week, no big act next — one piece taken hold of, one direction let carry it. What you get is a next few days you actually own, rather than one that owns you.
cells.sheetLine: You're choosing what's arriving, and the choice is holding.
cells.verb: let a second thing in and let one direction carry both streams
cells.place: the doorway where what's arriving steps in and gets met

cells.tense: You're bracing for a joining that hasn't landed yet, planning the meeting before anything has actually stepped through the door.
cells.ask: Before touching what's arriving, tend one ordinary thing that's already here — water it, mend it, finish it — and let that be the whole task.
cells.core:
What's coming in is allowed to arrive at its own speed, and what flows from it flows out of what you've already lived through, not what you're hoping for next. You meet it with a full hand, not an empty one, and that's what makes the meeting generous.

Right now you're rushing the meeting. You're shaping the joining ahead of time — imagining who or what will land, rehearsing how you'll fold it in — and the bracing has become more effort than the thing itself would ask for. It might be holding something worth keeping: not moving first feels like the door will close. What comes from doing less is the next arrival being able to show its true face instead of the one you drafted for it.

cells.tense: A joining that already happened is still standing at the door behind you, and the deciding hasn't been let through.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, your own honest read of one thing already inside — what it is for you — and let the deciding wait until after it's said.
cells.core:
What's inside has already been sorted through, and what you imagine next grows from that sorted ground — dreaming because what happened has been fully taken in, not because it's still being held off. You know what's true here without needing to argue it, and that read carries.

What isn't landing is the deciding. Something's already through the door, and you haven't let yourself call it what it is — so the next thing can't come in as a whole stream, only as more of the same standing water. Calling it plainly, with no plans attached, puts the first true thing back in motion; even a quiet read-out to yourself lets the coming thing arrive into a current instead of a pool. You get a next arrival you can actually meet, not one you keep holding off.
cells.sheetLine: What already came through is still waiting on your side of the door.

cells.place: the doorway where what's arriving steps in and gets met

cells.tense: Below what you'd say out loud, you're letting something in and letting it shape your direction — the pen is moving in this room whether or not you've claimed it.
cells.ask: Write one plain sentence — 'I let this in' — about a single thing you've been treating as something that just happened, and leave the sentence where you can see it.
cells.core:
Looking at what's here comes first and does its own quiet job — not to settle a worry or to earn calm, but because seeing clearly makes room for what's next. You can name what you're taking in, and that naming is what keeps a narrowing focus from turning into a forced one.

What's going on already is that a second stream is coming into your direction — someone's voice, some current, some pull — and getting folded in as if it were simply the conditions. This is occurring under the level of your own words, and it's this that steers, not the conditions. What the sentence gives back isn't a confession; it's a grip that's been there all along, and once it's on paper you can see whether you want to keep it or put it down.

attempts.check: The undrawn thing in my draft is the other person: a cell cannot know there is anyone else, whether they lean in or drift, or what a stream of feeling has been for the reader, so every glimpse of a 'verse' in these cells stays a glimpse and the acts stay inside the reader's own hands. A reader who is fine alone, or whose recent change feels pure loss, can still use everything here: the asks are single doable acts that teach something even if the read is wrong. The line that would serve the writer more than the reader is any sentence about 'the room' or 'the flow' that explains the method instead of standing the person on what is already arriving; those I trimmed to plain speech, and I kept 'flow' only where the card itself says two streams one flow, because in this house the flow is true and not a picture to be barred.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft was the outer results — no cell can know what a joining actually brought, so the cells speak only to what happens at the doorway: the meeting, the pace, the claiming. If the read is wrong about a person, the asks still teach: the reader can pick one entering thing, or speak one honest sentence, and learn something about pace or noticing that isn't dependent on my grasp of their situation. The line that risks serving the writer more than the reader is any sentence where the joining is pictured as a success — I've kept every picture as a moment of meeting, not an outcome, so the person can hand it back.
